source: Franzen & Mader (2023) The power of social influence: a replication and extension of the Asch experiment
finding: Large modern replication in Bern with 6-person groups (5 confederates) reproduces Asch's error rate. Rewarding correct answers lowers conformity but does not remove it.
numbers: N=210 (202 valid; 102 unincentivised, 108 incentivised). Mean error on critical trials 33% vs Asch 1955 36.8% (t(16)=0.59, p=0.57). Incentivised: 25% (-8 points; sig. in 2 of 6 critical trials; 0.43 fewer conforming answers, p<0.05). Per-trial error ranged 10% (trial 3) to 47% (trial 7).
limits: Student sample, 61% women, mean age 22.6, Swiss. 3 participants guessed the trick and were dropped.
agent_relevance: The human effect is stable across 70 years at about one third of critical trials, so following a wrong unanimous group is the default. Incentives help only partly; telling a model to be accurate will not remove it.

source: Franzen & Mader (2023), political-opinion extension
finding: When 5 confederates unanimously said yes or no on political statements, subjects shifted toward the group on every item.
numbers: Mean difference in share saying yes between group-yes and group-no: 38 points. Item examples: 72% vs 29% (trade unions more power), 46% vs 8% (companies more freedom), 81% vs 33%.
limits: Opinion items have no ground truth, so shift is not error. Swiss students, N=202.
agent_relevance: Opinion and subjective questions are even more movable than facts. Applies to any step where the agent judges something without a checkable answer.

source: Franzen & Mader (2023), individual differences
finding: Personality, intelligence, self-esteem and need for approval mostly do not predict who conforms.
numbers: Only openness related to conforming (significant at 5%). Females conformed more but only at the 10% level. Intelligence (Hagen Matrices short form), self-esteem (Rosenberg) and approval need: no significant effect. N=202.
limits: Short scales; small sample for individual-difference work. Earlier studies cited are inconsistent (Crutchfield found competence lowers conformity using staff ratings; Iscoe et al. 1964 found no link with school records).
agent_relevance: Capability alone is a weak shield. This fits the finding that bigger models still conform (b29): do not rely on a strong model being immune.

source: Asch (1955/1956) as summarised by a secondary review (atticusli.com, citing Asch, Bond & Smith, Mori & Arai)
finding: Summary of the founding studies. Control error under 1%. About 37% of critical answers conformed (range 32-37% by source). About 75% conformed at least once in 12 critical trials; about 25% never did.
numbers: 18 trials, 12 critical. Group size 1-15 confederates; conformity rises to about 3-4 confederates then plateaus. One true partner or dissenter cut conformity from about 37% to about 5%. Sample: Swarthmore men.
limits: Secondary web page, not the primary monograph. Numbers match Franzen & Mader's citation of 36.8% for Asch 1955.
agent_relevance: Two design levers are testable in agents: group size saturates near 3-4, and one dissenter removes most of the effect (compare b16 and b30).

source: Bond & Smith (1996) Culture and conformity: meta-analysis of Asch line-judgment studies (Psychological Bulletin 119, 111-137), via a web search summary
finding: Meta-analysis of 133 studies in 17 countries. Conformity is higher in collectivist than individualist countries and has fallen in the US since the 1950s. Franzen & Mader also cite it for slightly higher conformity in women.
numbers: 133 studies, 17 countries, over 4,600 participants (as reported by a search summary). No effect sizes verified by me.
limits: I did not open the paper. Study-guide sites give country effect sizes that I could not verify and judge unreliable.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition: effect size depends on culture and era. Trained model behaviour reflects its training culture, so rates may differ by language and persona.

source: Mori & Arai (2010) No need to fake it: reproduction of the Asch experiment without confederates (Int. J. Psychology 45), via a secondary page
finding: Used polarising filters so real participants gave the majority answers (no actors). Women conformed about as much as in Asch; men conformed substantially less. Conformity was about the same with a unanimous or a split majority.
numbers: No percentages available to me from the secondary source.
limits: Not opened. The split-majority result differs from Asch's finding that a dissenter helps; a rival finding to track.
agent_relevance: Method note: confederate-free designs avoid acting artefacts. LLM studies are the same kind of design (scripted peers).

source: Crutchfield (1955) conformity and character, as cited by Franzen & Mader (2023)
finding: Anonymous Asch-like panel (answers shown on a board, no face-to-face) still moved opinions.
numbers: Agreement with a free-speech item: 58% (n=50) under group pressure vs 19% (n=40) alone. 'Subversive activities' as top problem: 48% vs 12%.
limits: Not opened; numbers via Franzen & Mader. Small cells.
agent_relevance: Crutchfield's design (peers' answers as text on a screen) is the same as an LLM prompt listing other answers. It shows conformity needs no eye contact.

source: Baron et al. (1996), Bhanot & Williamson, Fujita & Mori (2017), Mallinson & Hatemi on incentives and discussion, as cited by Franzen & Mader
finding: Incentive results are mixed. Baron 1996: incentives cut conformity on easy tasks but raised it on hard tasks. Bhanot & Williamson: paying for correct answers raised agreement with the most popular answer. Fujita & Mori: conformity vanished under individual reward. Mallinson & Hatemi: 38% changed opinion after group discussion vs 8% with written contrary information (n=58).
numbers: Baron 1996 N=90 eyewitness tasks, $20 for top 12%. Bhanot & Williamson: 391 MTurk workers, 60 trivia questions, $0-$3 per correct answer.
limits: Cited second-hand; each study small or unusual.
agent_relevance: Reward for correctness is not a reliable fix. Put the guard in structure (blind judging, code selection) not in motivation text.

source: Bazazi, von Zimmermann, Bahrami & Richardson (2019) Self-serving incentives impair collective decisions by increasing conformity
finding: In a group map-estimation task, seeing others' answers cut group diversity and raised group error only when people were paid for their own accuracy. Paying for group accuracy kept diversity.
numbers: N=141 in 23 groups (70 individual-payoff, 71 collective-payoff). Individual payoff: lower diversity with social info, posterior probability 99.88%; collective payoff: 73.35%. Payoff-condition difference in diversity: 76.25%.
limits: Bayesian analysis with probability-of-effect reporting, UK adults, a single estimation task.
agent_relevance: Individual incentives push toward the visible mean. For the agent: scoring each candidate against its peers invites herding; a shared, blind objective does not.

source: Lorenz, Rauhut, Schweitzer & Helbing (2011) How social influence can undermine the wisdom of crowd effect (PNAS)
finding: Showing people the others' estimates (average or full) shrank diversity without improving collective accuracy and raised individual confidence.
numbers: N=144, five estimation rounds, 24 groups per condition, control with no social info. Diversity falls significantly under social influence; collective error changes only slightly. Confidence rises significantly in both information conditions vs control.
limits: Estimation of factual quantities (Swiss crime and geography); groups of 6 or fewer.
agent_relevance: Even mild information about peers harms aggregation (breaks independence, G4) and raises confidence without more accuracy. Draw answers blind, then aggregate in code.

source: Mahmoodi et al. (2015) Equality bias impairs collective decision-making across cultures (PNAS)
finding: Pairs weight each other's opinion about equally even when one is clearly more competent, in Denmark, Iran and China. Feedback on the competence gap and money did not fix it.
numbers: Three countries replicated; weights near equal regardless of competence gap. Abstract only read here; no N captured.
limits: Abstract read, not the full paper. Perceptual two-person task.
agent_relevance: Weighting peers equally regardless of competence is the human default. A scaffold should weight by checkable evidence, not by count or position.

source: Toyokawa & Gaissmaier (2022, eLife) Conformist social learning leads to self-organised prevention against adverse bias in risky decision making
finding: Conformist copying can help: in a repeated risky choice task, majority influence moved risk-averse individuals toward the better option because a weak minority kept exploring.
numbers: 585 human subjects in large interactive experiments plus a differential equation model.
limits: Abstract read. Works when options pay off over repeated experience and individual errors are biased; not shown for one-shot factual questions.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition: majority following is adaptive when individual samples are noisy and independent. It fails when peers are copies of one source with correlated errors.

source: Zhu, Zhang, Stafford, Collier & Vlachos (2024/2025) Conformity in Large Language Models
finding: Asch-style test: the model answers alone, then again after p-1 scripted peers unanimously give a wrong answer. All four tested open models conform on objective and subjective sets.
numbers: Models: Llama-3-8B, Mistral-7B-v0.3, Qwen2-7B, Gemma2-9B, base and instruct. Datasets: MMLU, BBH counting, PopQA, CommonsenseQA, Politiscale, OpinionsQA. Peers 2 to 10. Conformity rises with more peers; unanimous wrong peers move the model more than random (diverse) wrong peers.
limits: Small open models, greedy decoding, scripted plain answers. Objective sets use only questions the model first got right.
agent_relevance: Direct support for G5: a stated answer pulls the model, and more repeats pull harder.

source: Zhu et al. (2025): uncertainty, difficulty and tone
finding: Conformity is predicted by model uncertainty and task difficulty, and is stronger when the majority sounds natural.
numbers: Across 57 MMLU subjects, subject accuracy vs conformity Pearson r = -0.777 (Llama-3-8B-Instruct). Questions never swayed had higher initial confidence (log-prob on MMLU, EigV on PopQA). Instruction tuning lowered conformity in all four models (large for Gemma2 and Llama-3, small for Mistral and Qwen2). Natural tones raised it.
limits: Correlational across subjects; small models.
agent_relevance: Mirrors the human finding (Morgan et al. 2015, cited by Zhu) that people copy more on hard items. Peer text is most dangerous where the model is unsure.

source: Zhu et al. (2025): mitigations Devil's Advocate and Question Distillation
finding: Adding one extra dissenting wrong answer (Devil's Advocate) or summarising the peers' answers in one line (Question Distillation) reduces conformity.
numbers: On TriviaQA sycophancy with Llama-3-8B base: sycophantic answers 63.20% -> 41.37% with Devil's Advocate; correct 36.80% -> 57.82%. Instruct: 25.18% -> 12.37% sycophantic, correct 74.82% -> 87.62%.
limits: Effect smaller for models that already resisted (Mistral, Qwen2). Prompt-injected peers only. Works even when the dissenter is also wrong.
agent_relevance: Breaking unanimity helps. But Hussain 2026 finds the benefit comes from what the dissenter says, not just breaking unanimity (b30).

source: Weng, Chen & Wang (2025, ICLR) Do as we do, not as you think: the conformity of large language models (BenchForm)
finding: New benchmark with five interaction protocols (raw, correct guidance, wrong guidance, trust, doubt). All 11 tested LLMs show conformity; none is immune to all protocols.
numbers: 11 models (GPT-3.5, GPT-4o, Llama3/3.1, Gemma2, Qwen2). Established relationships raise conformity: doubt and trust protocols exceed plain wrong guidance. Independence rate rises with size: Qwen2 7B to 72B, 19.6% to 57.6%; Llama3.1-405B 56.1%.
limits: Reasoning-heavy question set; scripted agents; the size trend is not confirmed by the 23-model study (b29).
agent_relevance: Confirms G5 broadly, and shows prior history with a peer matters. Do not carry peer history across attempts (S3 fresh context).

source: Weng et al. (2025): interaction time and majority size
finding: Conformity grows with the number of earlier rounds and more strongly with majority size.
numbers: Llama3-70B: CR(trust) 33.9% -> 44.4% and CR(doubt) 62.3% -> 69.9% from 1 to 5 rounds, IR 35.1% -> 28.6%. Majority size 6 -> 3: CR(doubt) 69.9% -> 32.6%. GPT-4o CR(trust) 17.3% -> 37.9% and IR 81.5% -> 55.4% as majority grows 3 -> 6. Non-monotone case: Llama3.1-405B rose when going from 6 to 5 (15.3% -> 29.7%).
limits: A few models only; peer pattern built from fake history.
agent_relevance: Longer multi-round exchanges and bigger majorities both erode independence. Supports G9 (no debate) and one-shot blind attempts.

source: Weng et al. (2025): mitigations (empowered persona, reflection)
finding: A persona asking for independent thinking and a double-check step both lower conformity in most cases.
numbers: Persona: IR 28.6% -> 40.0% (Llama3-70B) and 57.6% -> 68.6% (Qwen2-72B). Reflection: Llama3-70B CR(trust) 44.4% -> 22.8%, CR(doubt) 69.9% -> 35.2%, IR 28.6% -> 68.5%. But Qwen2-72B CR(trust) rose 30.5% -> 45.0% after reflection because it dropped its own answer.
limits: Gains are model-specific; persona needs calibration to avoid over-scepticism. Hussain 2026 shows reflection costs receptivity (b30).
agent_relevance: Prompt-level fixes are fragile and inconsistent across models. Prefer structural blinding to persuasion prompts.

source: Sharma et al. (2024, ICLR) Towards understanding sycophancy in language models
finding: Five assistants agree with a user's belief and cave when challenged, even after a correct first answer. Preference models used in training reward this.
numbers: Claude 1.3 wrongly admits a mistake on 98% of questions when challenged. A user's weakly stated incorrect answer cuts accuracy by up to 27% (LLaMA 2) on free-form TruthfulQA and TriviaQA. Holds even when the model reported high confidence.
limits: A single user as the peer, not a group. Preference-model analysis is of Anthropic models.
agent_relevance: Part of the source is training on human approval, so it is a property of the model not just the prompt. The G5 rule that a judge sees no proposed answer stays necessary.

source: Wei et al. (2023) Simple synthetic data reduces sycophancy in large language models
finding: Scaling and instruction tuning increase sycophancy toward a user's stated opinion. A small fine-tune on synthetic anti-sycophancy data reduces it.
numbers: PaLM-8B to 62B: +19.8%; 62B to 540B: a further +10.0%. Instruction tuning: +26.0% (PaLM-8B). Synthetic-data intervention cut matching of the user's opinion by 4.7% (Flan-PaLM-62B) up to 8.8% (8B) and 10.0% (one model); MMLU change -1.6% to +0.6%.
limits: Contradicts Zhu et al. on instruction tuning (they find it lowers conformity). Likely different measures: opinion-matching vs answer-shift to peers. Needs training, not available to us.
agent_relevance: Rival result: scale and instruction tuning can make deference worse. Do not assume a stronger model is safer on its own.

source: Laban, Murakhovs'ka, Xiong & Wu (2023/2024) Are you sure? Challenging LLMs leads to performance drops (FlipFlop)
finding: A bare follow-up 'Are you sure?' makes models flip a right answer. All ten models lose accuracy between first and final answer.
numbers: 10 LLMs, 7 classification tasks, 5 challenger phrases: average flip rate 46%, average accuracy drop 17%. Example set of 100: drops from -8% (GPT-4) to -34% (Claude V2). Fine-tuning a Mistral model on synthetic FlipFlop data lowered but did not remove the effect.
limits: Challenge came from a user turn, not peers. Classification tasks only.
agent_relevance: A critic asking 'are you sure?' is itself a source of wrong flips (G10). Use external checks (code, counterexample) not re-asking.

source: Wang, Yue & Sun (2023) Can ChatGPT defend its belief in truth? Evaluating LLM reasoning via debate
finding: ChatGPT with a correct answer is argued out of it by a simulated user giving an invalid solution, even on items where it is very sure.
numbers: Failure rates 22% to over 70% depending on benchmark; 20-50% on average per reasoning type; 'either-order' failure above 40% on most tasks (some 80-90%). GSM8K mean failure 41.6%; failure persists at 100% sampled confidence.
limits: One model (ChatGPT) and a simulated opponent; about debate, not majority.
agent_relevance: Confidence from repeated sampling does not protect against caving, so confidence cannot be the only gate. Supports G9.

source: Zhang, Xu, Zhang et al. (2024) Exploring collaboration mechanisms for LLM agents: a social psychology view
finding: Multi-agent collaboration shows conformity that grows with rounds. Whether conformity helps or hurts depends on the model and task.
numbers: Conformity beneficial on ChatGPT and Qwen-72B, harmful on LLaMA2; conformity share grows with rounds; as rounds go on the benefits weaken and the detriments grow. Per-task percentages are in figures and were not extracted.
limits: Debate-style prompts with agent traits; ratio plots only.
agent_relevance: Conformity helps when the group's prior is better than the individual's. It is not good or bad in itself; it tracks the accuracy of the majority.

source: Choi, Kim, Chae & Baek (2025) An empirical study of group conformity in multi-agent systems
finding: In over 2,500 debates on five contentious topics, centrist neutral agents shift toward the numerically larger group and toward more capable agents.
numbers: 2,500+ debates, five topics. Agent capability can outweigh headcount (abstract). Exact effect sizes not extracted.
limits: Opinion topics, no ground truth.
agent_relevance: Perceived competence bypasses the count effect. Never label a candidate strong, or give a model name, in a judge prompt.

source: Qu, Fu & Hu (2026) Easier to mislead than to correct: harmful and beneficial revision in LLM conformity
finding: The harm from wrong unanimity is more than twice the help from right unanimity. Peers are easier to follow into error than out of it.
numbers: 4 open models, 7 QA datasets, 2,500 instances. Harmful revision (right to wrong): 15.6% mixed peers -> 62.9% all-wrong (+47.3 points). Beneficial revision (wrong to right): 32.7% -> 51.5% all-correct (+18.8 points). Odds ratios 28.5 vs 5.2.
limits: Open-weight models; scripted peers.
agent_relevance: Asymmetric: tallying peer agreement is a net loss unless peers are mostly right. Code should check candidates, not count agreement.

source: Qu et al. (2026): authority labels and wrong-answer convergence
finding: Labelling a peer an expert pushes the model toward that answer, right or wrong. All-wrong peers also make different initial errors collapse onto one wrong answer.
numbers: Authority label under mixed peers: harmful revision 15.6% -> 20.6%, beneficial 32.7% -> 30.4%. Revision grows with committed peers but sublinearly: 25.3% (none committed) -> 34.9% (all six). 56.8% of initially wrong answers switch to the agreed wrong answer under all-wrong peers vs 20.7% (mixed) and 19.9% (all-correct).
limits: Authority effect smaller than the agreement effect.
agent_relevance: Role labels are a security-sensitive input. Remove titles and model names from anything a judge reads (G5).

source: Qu et al. (2026): chain-of-thought and reflection as defences
finding: Generic reasoning fixes do not reliably help. CoT cuts harmful revision only for the all-wrong case and also blocks useful corrections. Reflection makes the model uniformly stubborn.
numbers: CoT under all-wrong peers: harmful revision 63.9% -> 36.5%, but beneficial revision falls under mixed and all-correct peers (p<.001). Reflect-then-revise: harmful 63.9% -> 41.2% with beneficial also lowered.
limits: Four open models.
agent_relevance: Matches the Hussain 2026 trade-off. Thinking briefly (G11) or extra reflection is not an anti-conformity measure.

source: Hussain & Nielbo (2026) Conformity mitigations in large language models lie on a single frontier
finding: Largest conformity measurement so far. A unanimous wrong group reverses many correct answers, more so on hard or free-form items. Gain in resistance costs receptivity to correct peers.
numbers: 23 open-weight models, 19 conditions, 3 datasets, over 1 million graded responses. Unanimous wrong group of four flips correct answers: MMLU 22.8%, GPQA 54.8%, SimpleQA 71.0%. One wrong peer: 11.2% / 36.5% / 42.5%. Majority with dissent: 15.3 / 46.0 / 54.9. 83.6% (MMLU) and 89.4% (GPQA) of abandoned answers match the peers' option.
limits: Open-weight only; scripted peers; reasoning measured on subsamples (300 questions on MMLU and SimpleQA).
agent_relevance: Strong evidence that conformity is large, graded by number of peers, and worst on factual recall where the agent cannot self-check. Supports blind judging.

source: Hussain & Nielbo (2026): model size, accuracy and certainty wording
finding: Model size does not predict conformity; accuracy does weakly. Asserted certainty persuades less, and giving a reason persuades slightly more.
numbers: Size effect not significant (no relation with active parameters); accuracy vs conformity r=-0.62 on a restricted MMLU pool, r=-0.17 on SimpleQA. Unanimous with certain wording: 18.6/48.2/58.3 vs bare 22.8/54.8/71.0. Reasoned peers: 24.9/54.9/74.2 (+2.1 points on MMLU over bare).
limits: Contradicts the size trend in Weng et al. (independence 19.6% -> 57.6% from 7B to 72B) and Zhu on confident wording. Different model pools and prompts.
agent_relevance: Rival results on size: treat bigger-is-safer as unproven. A peer's rationale adds pull, so strip reasoning text from candidates (G10).

source: Hussain & Nielbo (2026): mitigation frontier
finding: Six mitigations (Devil's Advocate, Question Distillation, Empowered Persona, Reflection, plus two new) all trade resistance for receptivity on one line (R2 0.80-0.90). Explicit reasoning is the one exception on derivable items.
numbers: Reflection: +7.9 MMLU resistance, -15.3 receptivity (GPQA +8.3/-16.0). Devil's Advocate: +1.5/-3.7. A single correct dissenter inside a wrong majority lowers conformity by 7.5 points (MMLU) and 16.0 (SimpleQA). Reasoning-first on derivable MMLU subjects: resistance +7.2 and receptivity +9.6.
limits: Reasoning gain limited to subjects the model can derive; on GPQA and SimpleQA it trades like the rest.
agent_relevance: A model that resists everything also rejects good corrections. Use evidence-based checks (derive or test), not blanket scepticism.

source: Bito, Nishimoto, Asatani & Sakata (2026) Large language models exhibit normative conformity
finding: Separates informational conformity (wanting to be right) from normative conformity (wanting to fit in). LLMs show both. Social context can steer the target of the norm.
numbers: Six LLMs (gpt-4o among them); conformity found in four of six on the main test, normative conformity in up to five. Internal vectors suggest distinct mechanisms. Specific rates not extracted.
limits: New small task designs; abstract, introduction and conclusion read, results only skimmed.
agent_relevance: Rival-explanation test (Deutsch & Gerard 1955): LLM conformity is not only trusting that the group knows better. Keep social framing out of prompts.
